summary: Markian Pergat, owner of Ottawa wood-restoration company Sand & Stain, explains how he went from doing every deck himself to a hands-off business by building a ClickFunnels sales funnel, running Facebook ads and firing himself from one role at a time. He and David DiNardo compare the technician path with the entrepreneur path, break down why most brokered businesses never sell, and map out how AI agents, licensing and personal brands change what a boring home-services business can become.
takeaways: Markian's three-month test: if you left your business for three months in peak season, would it collapse, stall or grow? Only the last answer means it is sellable.

One winter of building a ClickFunnels landing page plus Facebook ads took Sand & Stain from roughly $30,000 of solo work to over $100,000 booked before the season opened on May 1, which forced him to hire about 10 people at once.
Fire yourself from the jobs you hate first, then hand off production to a promoted manager; sales is the last role to give up, and Markian eventually replaced it with an online quoting calculator.
David's rule for owner-technicians: if an employee in your trade earns $100,000, you should be netting $200,000 as the owner or the stress of running the business is not worth it.
Markian cites the 80–90% of listed businesses that never sell; brokers get paid on the transaction, so they list you before the exit prep is done and rarely help you fix what a buyer will reject.

Know your SDE (seller's discretionary earnings) for a main-street business or EBITDA for a larger one; buyers value earnings, not revenue, and want two years of financials showing a manager, not the owner, running things.

Markian removes the brand name from the franchise formula (name, model, monetization) so he can license the Sand & Stain System and AI-agent stack to other painters without the reputation risk of a franchise.
